Robert Peel. A reforming Conservative who modernized British policing and shattered his own party over free trade.

Peel founded the Metropolitan Police in 1829 as Home Secretary, establishing the modern model of civilian policing. London constables became known as Bobbies after him, a legacy that endured. He served as Prime Minister twice, first from 1834 to 1835 and again from 1841 to 1846, using both terms to reposition the Tories as a party of progressive order rather than landed aristocracy.

His most consequential act came in 1846 when he repealed the Corn Laws to alleviate the Irish Potato Famine, breaking with protectionist Tory doctrine and putting humanitarian need above party loyalty. The repeal destroyed the Conservative Party's cohesion. Protectionists split off, and the free-trade faction evolved into the modern Liberal Party, fundamentally reshaping British politics.

Throughout his career, Peel articulated a vision of Conservatism grounded in gradual, lawful reform to prevent violent revolution. This philosophy guided his approach to governance even when it meant alienating his political base. In 1850, he died following a riding accident, mourned as a statesman who had put principle before party survival.
